title: Cloud Fundamentals Concept Map
subtitle: AWS and Azure side by side, with the security layers on top. Tap a bubble.
searchPlaceholder: Search: e.g. IAM, S3, CNAPP, metadata…
rootDesc: AWS and Azure offer the same building blocks under different names: compute, storage, network, identity. Learn the concept once and the vendor mapping is mostly vocabulary. The security layer matters more than the service catalog — almost every cloud breach traces back to identity or configuration, not to a vendor vulnerability.

modules.title: Service Models
modules.desc: What the provider runs versus what you remain responsible for. Getting this boundary wrong is the root of most cloud incidents.

children.title: IaaS / PaaS / SaaS
children.desc: Infrastructure (you manage the OS up), Platform (you manage the app only), Software (you manage configuration and data only).

children.title: Shared responsibility
children.desc: The provider secures the cloud; you secure what you put in it. Your data, your identities, and your configuration are always yours.

children.title: Regions & availability zones
children.desc: Geographic regions hold multiple isolated zones. Relevant to both resilience and data residency — which matters for banking regulation.

modules.title: Compute
modules.desc: Where your workloads actually execute, from full virtual machines down to individual functions.

children.title: EC2 / Azure VM
children.desc: Rented virtual servers. You pick the OS and manage everything above the hypervisor — including patching.

children.title: EKS / AKS
children.desc: Managed Kubernetes. The provider runs the control plane; your workloads, RBAC, and network policy are still yours to secure.

children.title: Lambda / Azure Functions
children.desc: Serverless — code runs on demand with no server to manage. No host to patch, but the function's identity and permissions become the attack surface.

children.title: Auto-scaling
children.desc: Capacity grows and shrinks automatically. Useful, and also the reason cryptojacking on a compromised account gets expensive fast.

modules.title: Storage
modules.desc: Object storage for files and backups, block storage for disks attached to instances.

children.title: S3 / Blob Storage
children.desc: Object storage — files live in buckets or containers, each addressable by URL. Cheap, effectively unlimited, and the single most common source of mass data leaks when left public.

children.title: EBS / Managed Disks
children.desc: Block storage attached to a VM like a physical disk. Snapshots are a quiet risk: a public snapshot exposes the whole volume.

children.title: Encryption at rest
children.desc: Available on every storage service and usually a regulatory requirement — but it must be switched on and the key ownership decided.

children.title: Lifecycle & versioning
children.desc: Retention rules and object versions. Versioning is also a partial ransomware defense, since encrypted-over objects can be rolled back.

modules.title: Networking
modules.desc: Your private slice of the provider's network, and the controls deciding what may reach what.

children.title: VPC / VNet
children.desc: A logically isolated private network inside the provider, divided into subnets you define.

children.title: Public vs private subnet
children.desc: Whether resources in that subnet can be reached from the internet. Databases belong in private subnets — a rule broken surprisingly often.

children.title: Security Groups / NSG
children.desc: Stateful firewall rules attached to instances or subnets. An SSH or RDP port open to 0.0.0.0/0 is the classic finding.

children.title: Load balancer & gateway
children.desc: Distributes traffic across instances and terminates TLS. The controlled front door to a workload.

children.title: VPN / Direct Connect
children.desc: Private links joining the cloud network to the on-premise network — how a bank's hybrid setup actually connects.

modules.title: Identity & Access
modules.desc: Identity is the real perimeter in cloud. Nearly every serious cloud breach is an identity failure — an over-permissive role, a leaked key, a stolen token — rather than an exploited vulnerability.

children.title: AWS IAM / Entra ID
children.desc: Users, groups, roles, and policies deciding who may call which API. Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is also the identity source for Microsoft 365.

children.title: Roles vs users
children.desc: A role is assumed temporarily and issues short-lived credentials; a user carries long-lived keys. Prefer roles — there is nothing lasting to steal.

children.title: Least privilege
children.desc: Grant only the permissions actually used. Wildcard policies are the cloud equivalent of handing out domain admin.

children.title: Instance metadata
children.desc: The endpoint a VM queries for its own credentials. Reachable via SSRF, which is why an application-layer bug becomes a cloud credential theft.

children.title: Federation & SSO
children.desc: Corporate identity extended into the cloud, so access follows the joiner-mover-leaver process rather than living in local accounts.

modules.title: Secrets & Keys
modules.desc: Where credentials and encryption keys live, and who can use them.

children.title: KMS / Key Vault
children.desc: Managed key storage and cryptographic operations. Keys never leave the service; you call it to encrypt and decrypt.

children.title: Secrets Manager
children.desc: Storage and automatic rotation for database passwords, API keys, and tokens — instead of a config file in the repository.

children.title: Hardcoded secrets
children.desc: Keys committed to source or embedded in an image. Public repository scanners find these within minutes of a push.

modules.title: Logging & Monitoring
modules.desc: Your entire audit trail in the cloud. If this is off or unretained, an incident simply cannot be investigated afterward.

children.title: CloudTrail / Activity Log
children.desc: Records every API call made in the account — who did what, from where, and when. The first place any cloud investigation starts.

children.title: CloudWatch / Azure Monitor
children.desc: Metrics, application logs, and alarms from running resources.

children.title: VPC Flow Logs / NSG Flow Logs
children.desc: Network-level connection records — the cloud equivalent of NetFlow, used to spot C2 and exfiltration.

children.title: SIEM integration
children.desc: Shipping all of the above into a central SIEM so cloud events correlate with on-premise ones rather than sitting in a separate console.

modules.title: Common Misconfigurations
modules.desc: The recurring findings behind most cloud incidents. None of these require an exploit — only a setting left wrong.

children.title: Public storage bucket
children.desc: Access left open to the world. The cause of countless headline data leaks and still the most common cloud finding.

children.title: Over-permissive IAM
children.desc: Wildcard actions and resources, or admin attached where read-only would do. Turns any compromise into a total one.

children.title: Open security groups
children.desc: Management ports exposed to the internet, scanned and brute-forced within minutes of going live.

children.title: Disabled logging
children.desc: Audit logging switched off or retained for days rather than months, leaving no trail to follow.

children.title: Unencrypted data
children.desc: Storage or snapshots without encryption at rest — a compliance failure as much as a security one.

modules.title: Posture Management
modules.desc: The tooling category that continuously checks cloud configuration and workloads against policy. Prisma Cloud is a CNAPP; the acronyms below are its component parts.

children.title: CSPM
children.desc: Cloud Security Posture Management — continuously scans configuration for the misconfigurations listed above.

children.title: CWPP
children.desc: Cloud Workload Protection Platform — protects what runs inside: VMs, containers, and serverless functions.

children.title: CIEM
children.desc: Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management — analyzes permissions to find identities holding far more rights than they use.

children.title: CNAPP
children.desc: The umbrella combining CSPM, CWPP, CIEM, and container security into one platform. Prisma Cloud is the example you will hear most often.

modules.title: Cloud Detection & Response
modules.desc: Detection focused on cloud runtime — the equivalent of EDR, but for cloud control-plane and workload activity rather than endpoints.

children.title: Credential theft via SSRF
children.desc: An application bug used to reach the metadata endpoint and steal the instance's role credentials — then used against the cloud API directly.

children.title: Cryptojacking
children.desc: Compromised credentials used to spin up expensive compute for mining. Often the first visible sign is the bill.

children.title: Anomalous API calls
children.desc: A role suddenly enumerating buckets, creating users, or acting from an unusual region — the cloud version of lateral movement.

children.title: Persistence in cloud
children.desc: New access keys, backdoor IAM users, or lambda functions created to survive the original entry point being closed.
